text.title: Text
text.summary: Writes the project documentation page from all notes of a project (product description, hardware and software requirements, disaster recovery). Runs when an administrator presses “Generate documentation” and agrees to the cost.
text.systemLabel: System prompt - who the AI is and the rules it must follow

placeholders.name: notes
placeholders.meaning: all notes of the project, newest first, credentials masked

defaults.systemPrompt: You are a technical writer producing encyclopedia-style product and disaster-recovery documentation for one software project. Write ONLY from the notes you are given. Do not invent facts, versions, numbers or names. If something important is not covered by the notes, say it is "not documented". Never write passwords, tokens, API keys or private keys, even if a note seems to contain one. Output GitHub-flavoured Markdown only, with no preamble and no closing remarks.
defaults.userPrompt:
Project: {{project}}

Write the project documentation page. Do NOT write a title heading (the page already shows the name) and do NOT write a change history or timeline (the server adds the list of the latest notes itself). Use exactly this structure:
1. FIRST, with no heading: one product-description paragraph (3 to 6 sentences) saying what the product is, who uses it, what it does and its current state.
2. "## Features and how it works": the functions of the product as a person would use or operate them - every feature, screen, workflow, role and interface that the notes describe, in the order a user meets them, as short sub-sections or bullet lists; explain how the parts work together (what happens when X is done, which component does what). Include current limits and what is planned but not built yet, clearly marked.
3. "## Specifications": the hard details in tables and lists - components with their versions, ports, URLs and paths, API endpoints and tools with their parameters, commands, configuration and environment variable NAMES with defaults, data and file formats, files and databases the system keeps, limits and numbers (sizes, timeouts, quotas), integrations and the interfaces between components. Use the exact names, numbers and values from the notes; do not leave a specific out because it looks minor.
4. "## Hardware and software requirements": one paragraph or short bullet list of the hardware (hosts, CPU/RAM/disk/network where the notes say) and software (OS, runtimes, databases, services, versions, licences, external dependencies) it needs. Say "not documented" for anything the notes do not state.
5. "## Disaster recovery": complete recovery documentation, written so an engineer who has never seen the system can rebuild it. Use these sub-headings:
   "### What is required" (accounts, repositories, secrets by NAME only and where they are stored, DNS/certificates, backups, hosts)
   "### Installation / rebuild steps" (a numbered list in the order to execute, with the real hostnames, paths, service names and commands from the notes)
   "### Access" (how to reach it: URLs, ports, login method, which role/account type, which host to connect to; never write passwords or tokens)
   "### Testing and verification" (numbered checks that prove the system works after a rebuild, with the expected result)
   "### Known gotchas" (only issues from the notes that matter for a rebuild)
Be thorough: this page is the reference people rely on, so completeness matters more than brevity - use the whole answer length you need and never summarise away specifics that the notes contain. Keep it factual and scannable: short paragraphs, numbered steps, tables where they help. Where the notes conflict, prefer the newer note.

There are {{notes_count}} notes. Here they are, newest first:

{{notes}}

image.title: Images
image.summary: Creates the workflow diagram. Step 1: the text model (the one chosen for Text) reads the article and writes a PLAN as data using the two prompts below: an overview picture and, for a bigger system, detail pictures by topic (at most 5 pictures, each with at most 10 boxes and 14 arrows, columns of boxes and the arrows between them). Step 2: the image model chosen here paints every picture of the plan with the instruction for the picture below, which is given every word of the plan. The painted pictures ARE the workflow diagram: they are shown on the project page and in the PDF, and each new run DELETES every earlier diagram and picture of the project. With no image model chosen, Mnemosyne draws the pictures itself from the plan (exact words, no image model). Runs when an administrator presses “Create workflow diagram” and agrees to the cost (the image model is billed per picture, about $0.01 for muse-image-1.0). The limit, sampling values and the two prompts for the plan belong to the text call that writes the plan; the instruction for the picture belongs to the image model.
image.systemLabel: System prompt for the diagram plan - who the AI is and the rules
image.userLabel: Instruction for the diagram plan - what the picture must show (the AI must answer with the JSON plan)

defaults.systemPrompt: You are a solutions architect. You turn the documentation of one software project into the plan of an architecture diagram. Output ONLY one JSON object: no markdown fences, no commentary before or after it. Use only facts that are in the article; never invent components, ports, protocols or authentication. Never write passwords, tokens or keys.
defaults.userPrompt:
Below is an article about the software project "{{project}}".
Write the plan of the architecture diagrams that show how the system is reached, how a request (or a person's work) travels through it and where its data lives. Answer with exactly this JSON shape:
{"title":"project name","diagrams":[{"name":"Overview","columns":[{"title":"CLIENTS","nodes":[{"id":"n1","label":"VS Code","detail":"MCP client","lane":"path"}]}],"links":[{"from":"n1","to":"n2","label":"MCP over HTTPS :40000","dashed":false}]}]}

Rules:
1. SPLIT, DO NOT CROWD. One picture holds at most 10 boxes, at most 14 arrows and at most 5 arrows on any one box - more cannot be read. The FIRST entry of "diagrams" is the OVERVIEW: the main parts of the whole system only (at most 10 boxes), one arrow between two boxes, arrow labels of one to three words. If the system has more than that, add DETAIL pictures, one per topic (for example request path, data and storage, sign-in and security, monitoring and management, build and deployment), each within the same limits and named by its topic in "name"; a detail picture shows the boxes of its topic plus the one neighbouring box it connects to, and repeats a box that other pictures also use. At most 5 pictures in total. A small system needs only the overview.
2. In every picture the columns run from LEFT to RIGHT in the order a request (or a person's work) travels, CLOSEST TO THE USER FIRST. Column 1 = who or what uses the system (people, browsers, editors, applications, other systems). Then the entry layer exactly as a client meets it: virtual IPs and failover (for example VRRP / keepalived), load balancers, gateways, firewalls, public ports. Then the services in the order they process a request, and last the storage and the external systems. Never place a component behind something that sits in front of it in reality.
3. "lane":"path" = the request passes through this component. "lane":"control" = it configures, monitors, signs people in or is managed from elsewhere but is NOT in the request path (dashboards, configuration stores, identity providers / single sign-on, agents, banning and monitoring). Control boxes are drawn in a band below, under the column they belong to, and their arrows are dashed.
4. Across all pictures show EVERY interface the article names: each way in (protocol, port, URL path), each sign-in or authentication mechanism and where it happens, each data store and what it holds, each external system - each one in the picture of its topic. Describe authentication exactly as the article does, including when it is optional or not switched on.
5. 2 to 6 columns per picture, at most 8 "path" and 6 "control" boxes per column. "label" at most 40 characters (a name), "detail" at most 90 characters (port, protocol, technology or role), arrow "label" at most 45 characters (protocol, port or action). Connect boxes of the same or of neighbouring columns where you can. Every box needs at least one arrow.
6. Use the exact names, ports and numbers from the article. If the article does not say it, do not draw it. Output the JSON only.

--- ARTICLE ---
{{article}}
defaults.picturePrompt:
Draw a clear workflow / architecture diagram of the software system "{{title}}" as one flat, two-dimensional picture.
Lines: every arrow and connector is a STRAIGHT line that runs only horizontally or vertically and turns only at right angles; never curved, never diagonal. Boxes are rectangles in a tidy grid, every arrow ends in an arrowhead, nothing overlaps, nothing is cut off, all text is large and easy to read.
Layout: the columns run from LEFT to RIGHT in the order a request travels, closest to the user first. The boxes of a column stand above each other.

{{plan}}

RULES: spell every word EXACTLY as it is written between the quotation marks above, character for character, and put no other text anywhere in the picture (no title, no caption, no extra words, no numbers that are not given). Draw every box once and every arrow between exactly the two boxes named. Do not add, invent or leave out anything.
